name: VVenC
baseline: VTM-19.2 (JVET VVC reference encoder) and HM-17.0 (HEVC reference encoder); x265 v3.5 is also plotted but only in figures
workload: Random-access encoding of JVET common-test-condition HD and UHD sequences at QP 22/27/32/37, VVenC with 8 threads, reported as encoder runtime speedup together with PSNR BD-rate versus HM-17.0.
claimed_speedup: VVenC v1.14.0 Table III (HD4K): faster preset 2400x, fast 1100x, medium 330x, slow 87x, slower 19x faster than VTM-19.2 (HD column: 2400x/1100x/280x/74x/15x); versus HM-17.0 the same presets are 380x/180x/53x/14x/3x faster with PSNR BD-rate of -13.3%/-25.8%/-35.1%/-39.1%/-42.1%. Page text: slower preset reaches VTM-like BD-rate with more than 20x speedup over VTM. Speedups versus x265 are shown only as a figure (no numbers in text).
hardware: AMD EPYC 7502P 32-Core @2.5GHz (Dell servers); VVenC and x265 run with 8 threads, HM and VTM single-threaded
tradeoffs: Encodes H.266/VVC, whose decoder support and patent licensing differ from H.264/HEVC; the speedups are relative to the slow JVET reference software, not to a production encoder. Perceptual tuning (XPSNR-based QPA) is available.
caveats: First-party wiki numbers; compiler, flags and thread pinning not stated, so not reproducible-tier. The baselines in the numeric tables (VTM, HM) are research reference encoders and are single-threaded, so the headline multipliers (hundreds to thousands of x) say little about speed versus x265 or x264. The x265 v3.5 comparison (PSNR and MS-SSIM tuned, 8 threads) appears only as figures. Page cites peer-reviewed VVenC papers that were not opened (IEEE and ACM are blocked here). Page last edited 2026-03-30.
found_via: GitHub: WebFetch of https://github.com/fraunhoferhhi/vvenc (README links the Encoder Performance wiki page), then the wiki raw markdown

name: glint
baseline: FFmpeg native AAC encoder (libavcodec aac); the same league also times Fraunhofer FDK AAC, Apple afconvert, vo-aacenc and LAME 3.100 -q 2 (MP3)
workload: Encoding 6 audio clips (speech, electronic, quartet, industrial, piano, castanets) to AAC-LC at 128 and 256 kbps with the project's tests/compare_encoders.py league; speed reported as multiples of real time.
claimed_speedup: README: fastest encoder in the AAC league at every quality tier, about 272x / 168x realtime at -q speed / -q best on an M1 (MP3 about 260x / 34x). League log rows for ffmpeg native AAC vs glint -q normal: speech 128 kbps 56x vs 169x, electronic 128 kbps 46x vs 214x, electronic 256 kbps 25x vs 246x, quartet 128 kbps 89x vs 196x, industrial 128 kbps 84x vs 175x (about 2.1x to 9.8x faster across the 12 league rows, derived from page data). In the same log FDK reaches 105x-175x and Apple 80x-181x.
hardware: README says Apple M1 for the headline speed numbers; the league log itself does not state a CPU
tradeoffs: Clean-room MP3, AAC-LC and Opus encoders plus Opus, Vorbis, FLAC, MP3 and AAC decoders; C ABI with Python, Rust and Dart bindings; fixed-point builds for MCUs. Opus encoder is CELT-only. AAC quality at 128 kbps trails Apple and FDK on speech and electronic clips (noise-to-mask), beats FFmpeg native AAC.
caveats: Very new project (first commits July 2026, 322 commits, 2 stars) with first-party measurements only; compiler and flags not stated, CPU only named as M1 in README prose. Real-time multiples for ffmpeg-aac may include process start-up since the harness times the CLI (not confirmed). The README states glint's AAC tables were cross-checked against two independent implementations, but no third party has reproduced the speed table. Speed claim is for AAC; MP3 comparison is quality-first versus LAME.
found_via: WebSearch: "faster than libopus" OR "faster than LAME" OR "faster than libvorbis" audio encoder decoder github

name: LibFResample
workload: Resampling 16-bit stereo and mono audio from 48 kHz to 44.1 kHz, measured as multiples of real time on four machines.
claimed_speedup: Stereo, System C (3.2 GHz AMD Phenom II, GCC 4.7): LibFResample Q=5 Medium 1276x realtime vs libsamplerate Sinc Med. 35x and Sinc Fast 68x; Q=8 High 318x vs Sinc Best 8.5x; System D (1.7 GHz Core i5, Clang 4.0): Q=5 1247x vs Sinc Med. 39x. Mono Q=2 Low 3195x vs libsamplerate Linear 1112x (System D).
compiler_and_flags: GCC 4.4 (System A), GCC 4.0 (B), GCC 4.7 (C), Clang 4.0 (D); optimization flags not stated
hardware: 1.6 GHz Intel Atom, 2.0 GHz PowerPC G5, 3.2 GHz AMD Phenom II, 1.7 GHz Intel Core i5
tradeoffs: Only 16-bit mono/stereo input, no error reporting, SSE2 and AltiVec only, no Windows port; README itself says it is not release quality. Quality table: Q=5 gives 16.3 kHz bandwidth and 84 dB SNR, Q=8 19.5 kHz and 92 dB; filter is a plain Kaiser-windowed sinc.
caveats: Numbers are from 2005-2012 hardware and libsamplerate 0.1.8; libsamplerate later got speed work, and Q levels are not matched to libsamplerate's converters for equal SNR, so the comparison pairs by name only. The SRC throughput figures come from SRC's own test tool, divided by 44100. Baseline is not an FFmpeg component, so baseline_in_list is false. Last commit is over four years old.
found_via: WebSearch: "faster than libsamplerate" OR "faster than libsoxr" OR "faster than swresample" resampler github

name: dav1d
workload: Decoding 3840x2160 60 fps low-delay AV1 streams (about 10 Mbps; a game clip of 1200 frames and a camera clip of 1094 frames) at 4 and 6 threads.
claimed_speedup: Third-party PR measurement: game clip 74.7 fps (dav1d) vs 22.3 fps (libaom) at 4 threads (3.3x), 74.1 vs 26.0 at 6 threads (2.9x); camera clip 61.1 vs 20.2 at 4 threads (3.0x), 67.6 vs 22.1 at 6 threads (3.1x). PR text: libaom cannot decode 4K60 in real time (20-26 fps), dav1d is about 3x faster at the same thread count.
hardware: 2x Intel Xeon Silver 4114 @ 2.20 GHz (20C/40T, AVX2/AVX-512), 48 GB DDR4-2400, Ubuntu 22.04.5, kernel 6.8
stars_or_usage: 807 stars on the GitHub read-only mirror; origin is code.videolan.org/videolan/dav1d
tradeoffs: AV1 decoder only (no encoder); BSD-2-Clause; hand-written assembly for x86, ARM and others. The dav1d FAQ frames its speed goal with the analogy that a from-scratch decoder can beat the reference one the way ffvp9 beat libvpx.
caveats: The only numbers opened this session are from a pull request description by a third party (OvenMediaEngine PR #2336, dated 2026-09-27); benchmark scripts, compiler flags and exact build options are not in the PR, and the PR lists dav1d 1.5.4 and libaom 3.12.0 only in version files. The dav1d README and FAQ on the mirror carry no numbers. The origin repo on code.videolan.org was not opened. libaom is not an FFmpeg component, though FFmpeg wraps both decoders.
found_via: WebSearch: AV1 decoder OR encoder "faster than" libaom OR x265 benchmark site:github.com C++ SIMD

name: edge264
baseline: FFmpeg libavcodec H.264 decoder (README chart also shows LibAVC and OpenH264)
workload: Decoding the 1080p 10 s Big Buck Bunny H.264 clip (30 MB), wall-clock seconds, median of 5 runs, on x86-64 and arm64.
claimed_speedup: Values read from the README benchmark chart source (README-benchmark.svg, 'Decoding time measured on 27/07/2026', lower is better): x86-64 edge264 Clang 3.9 s, GCC 4.5 s, FFmpeg 4.6 s, LibAVC 6.4 s, OpenH264 8.2 s; arm64 edge264 Clang 3.8 s, GCC 3.9 s, FFmpeg 4.7 s, LibAVC 4.5 s, OpenH264 6.8 s (Clang build about 1.18x faster than FFmpeg on x86-64 and 1.24x on arm64, derived from page data). FOSDEM'24 talk title linked from README: reach 10% faster speed and 3x code reduction over the state of the art.
compiler_and_flags: Clang and GCC builds shown separately; versions and flags not stated
tradeoffs: Supports Progressive High and MVC 3D profiles only, 8-bit 4:2:0; interlaced, higher bit depths and 4:2:2 are planned. Uses compiler vector extensions instead of hand-written assembly (SSE and NEON from one code path, WASM via Clang). README targets API freeze in 2027.
caveats: Chart is an SVG whose numbers exist only as embedded labels (README text has no numbers); CPU model, FFmpeg version, FFmpeg thread settings and decoder flags are not stated. Stock edge264's multithreading is reported broken by the jens-duttke fork, whose own chart shows FFmpeg with multithreading decoding faster than edge264 multithreaded, so the win appears single-thread only. Library is pre-1.0.
found_via: WebSearch: github C++ H.264 OR HEVC OR ProRes OR MJPEG decoder "times faster than ffmpeg" OR "x faster than ffmpeg" OR "faster than libavcodec"

name: edge264-mvc
baseline: FFmpeg libavcodec H.264 decoder, single-threaded (1T) and multithreaded (MT)
workload: Decoding the 1080p 10 s Big Buck Bunny H.264 clip, wall-clock seconds, fastest of 10 runs, on GitHub-hosted runners (x86-64 and arm64), each decoder single-threaded and multithreaded.
claimed_speedup: Values read from the fork's README-benchmark.svg ('Decoding time measured on 19/09/2026'): x86-64 single-thread edge264-mvc Clang 3.9 s, GCC 4.1 s vs FFmpeg 4.8 s (about 1.23x faster for Clang, derived from page data); arm64 single-thread Clang 3.9 s, GCC 3.9 s vs FFmpeg 4.7 s. Multithreaded: edge264-mvc Clang 2.9 s (x86-64) and 2.6 s (arm64) vs FFmpeg 2.4 s and 2.0 s, so FFmpeg is faster with threads. LibAVC 1T 6.7/4.4 s, MT 4.9/2.6 s; OpenH264 8.4/6.6 s.
compiler_and_flags: Clang and GCC builds shown separately; the changelog says native builds pair -march=native with -mtune=generic; other flags not stated
hardware: GitHub-hosted CI runners (few vCPUs); CPU model not stated
stars_or_usage: 7 stars (fork); powers Oku3D Media Player and mvc-source per README
tradeoffs: Adds working multithreaded decoding (bit-exact to single-thread on the 231-stream JVT conformance corpus) and MVC 3D Blu-ray decoding that FFmpeg drops, plus many robustness fixes; same profile limits as edge264 (Progressive High and Stereo High, 8-bit 4:2:0).
caveats: Fork with performance-relevant changes (multithreading, native tuning flags); reported here because its chart separates single and multithreaded runs and shows the win over FFmpeg only holds single-threaded. CI-runner timings are noisy and vCPU-limited by the README's own note. CPU model and FFmpeg build details not stated.
found_via: WebSearch: github C++ H.264 OR HEVC OR ProRes OR MJPEG decoder ... (edge264 fork listed in results)

name: Shine (fixed-point MP3 encoder)
workload: Encoding a 5 min 18 s 44.1 kHz stereo WAV to 128 kbps MP3 with the shineenc CLI versus lame -b 128.
claimed_speedup: On a MacBook Pro (arm64, M1 Pro, 2022-12-30): Shine 318.0x realtime vs LAME 3.100 88.7x realtime (about 3.6x faster, derived from page data). Older outdated tests: Raspberry Pi Shine 3.6x vs LAME 1.8x realtime.
hardware: MacBook Pro arm64 M1 Pro (current numbers); Raspberry Pi and Nexus 5 (outdated)
tradeoffs: Fixed-point encoder for CPUs without an FPU; no psychoacoustic model, so quality at a given bitrate is below LAME; LGPL-2.0 (COPYING is GNU Library GPL v2). README notes the encoder may have latent bugs and that work on this fork was limited to reorganizing code into a shared API.
caveats: Single run timings from CLI output, no compiler flags, no quality parity (LAME runs full psychoacoustics with qval=3 while Shine does not), so the speed ratio compares different amounts of work. README describes this as a fork of Gabriel Bouvigne's old code; savonet/shine appears to resolve to the same repo (same star count). Last commit 2023-01-01 is just over three years old.
found_via: GitHub: raw README of toots/shine, found while checking audio-codec candidates (topic and search queries 'mp3 encoder')

name: uvgRTP
baseline: FFmpeg (libavformat RTP) and Live555 as RTP senders/receivers for HEVC video
workload: RTP streaming of 4K HEVC video over a 10 Gbps LAN: peak goodput (throughput without protocol overhead) and round-trip frame latency, measured with the public rtp-benchmarks framework.
claimed_speedup: Paper abstract (search snippet only, IEEE MMSP 2020): on an Intel Core i7-4770 uvgRTP streams HEVC at 5.0 Gb/s over a local 10 Gb/s network, with 4.4 times the peak goodput and 92.1% lower latency than FFmpeg, and over double the goodput and 82.3% lower latency than Live555.
hardware: Core i7-4770 and AMD Threadripper 2990WX connected by 10 Gbps LAN (rtp-benchmarks README); the paper reports the i7-4770 result
tradeoffs: RTP/SRTP/ZRTP library for HEVC, VVC, AVC and Opus transport; benchmarks cover RTP transport only, not codec speed. Linux benchmark scripts.
caveats: The numbers come from a search-result summary of the peer-reviewed MMSP 2020 paper; IEEE Xplore and the Tampere research portal were blocked, so the paper itself was not opened and the percentages could not be checked against its text. The rtp-benchmarks README carries the public framework and hardware but no results, says the FFmpeg and Live555 implementations have not been tested in a while, and sets no compiler flags. Paper results are from 2020 library versions. Tier B rests on peer review; downgrade to C if the paper cannot be confirmed.
found_via: WebSearch: uvgRTP RTP library goodput latency FFmpeg Live555 comparison results paper

name: Kvazaar
workload: HEVC encoding at comparable coding efficiency and presets with 8 and 16 threads (per the 2016 Kvazaar ACM Multimedia paper summary).
claimed_speedup: Search-snippet summaries of Kvazaar papers (not opened): 19% faster than x265 for the same coding efficiency with 8 threads and 38% faster with 16 threads at high-quality presets; at high-speed presets 4.5% better coding efficiency and about twice as fast as x265. Separate Jetson all-intra study snippet: 65.44% and 69.4% faster than x265 with 1.88% and 0.6% BD-rate improvement. The README itself carries no numbers.
tradeoffs: Open-source HEVC encoder from Tampere University's Ultra Video Group with x264-style preset names and a library API; also the base of the uvg266 VVC encoder. README says speed and RD quality are still improving.
caveats: Numbers are from search-result snippets of ResearchGate abstracts (blocked here), so snippet only; the 2016 comparison used a much older x265. GitHub issue #378 'kvazaar is not as fast as x265' reports a user could not reproduce the paper's speed claim (issue body only, no numbers visible). Treat as a lead to verify; tier C because neither the repo nor any opened page carries the numbers.
found_via: WebSearch: kvazaar OR "SVT-HEVC" OR "uvg266" vs x265 encoding speed fps benchmark results table github

name: opuspp
baseline: libopus 1.6.1 decoder (opus_decode_float), built with identical compiler and flags
workload: Decoding a 60 s mixed-audio stream (tones, noise, transients, orchestral music) encoded by libopus as 48 kHz fullband stereo, 10 ms CELT frames at 320 kb/s and encoder complexity 4; best of 7 passes pinned to one core, packet buffer flushed from cache before each pass. Other streams: 128 and 510 kb/s, 10% packet loss, complexity 0 and 2.
claimed_speedup: Like for like (same compiler and flags) opuspp is 1.27x to 1.48x faster than libopus at 320 kb/s (GCC Size 1.27x, GCC Balanced 1.48x, GCC Fast 1.43x, Clang Size 1.42x, Clang Balanced 1.46x, Clang Fast 1.42x); 1.09x to 1.50x across other bit rates, packet loss and encoder complexities. Five of six opuspp builds beat the fastest libopus build (GCC Fast) by 1.33x to 1.43x; GCC Size opuspp is slower than that build (0.88x).
compiler_and_flags: GCC 16.2 and Clang 22.1; Size: -Os, Balanced: -O2, Fast: -O3 -march=native -ffast-math -falign-loops=32 (libopus with OPUS_FLOAT_APPROX=ON and OPUS_FAST_MATH=ON, opuspp with OPUSPP_FLOAT_APPROX); all with -DNDEBUG -ffunction-sections -fdata-sections and -Wl,--gc-sections
hardware: One core of an AMD Ryzen 5 9600X
tradeoffs: Header-only freestanding C++23 decoder specialised to one stream type: CELT-only, fullband, 48 kHz stereo float output, 10 ms frames, prediction disabled, no pitch post-filter, no SILK, hybrid, FEC or DNN extensions. Bit-identical to libopus in strict-IEEE builds (47 encoder configurations, 300k-packet fuzz); the Fast profile is not bit-exact in either decoder. Smaller code (71-198 KB vs 98-236 KB static libopus) and decoder state (18.1 KB vs 26.6 KB), no heap or libm.
caveats: Brand-new repository written by Claude Code per its README (an AI-made port); benchmark is first-party and on one CPU (Ryzen 5 9600X), single synthetic 60 s stream; libopus reference built for the x86-64 baseline with SSE kernels per the verification doc. Only works for the narrow stream profile above, so it is not a general libopus replacement. Compiler versions (GCC 16.2, Clang 22.1) are as stated in the doc and were not independently checked. Results vary by a few percent between runs per the doc.
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/opus?l=c%2B%2B&o=desc&s=updated, then the README and docs/performance.md

name: libsoxr (SoX Resampler library)
baseline: libsamplerate (measured through the Python 'samplerate' package, sinc_medium and sinc_best)
workload: Downsampling 10 s of 48000 Hz audio to 44100 Hz, CPU time in ms, run on Google Colab by the python-soxr author (soxr called through the python-soxr wrapper).
claimed_speedup: python-soxr README speed table: soxr (HQ) 10.8 ms and soxr (VHQ) 14.5 ms vs samplerate (sinc_medium) 223 ms and samplerate (sinc_best) 794 ms, i.e. about 21x and 74x faster for HQ against those two settings (derived from page data). Same table: scipy.signal.resample 21.3 ms, resampy kaiser_fast 108 ms, kaiser_best 310 ms, torchaudio 13.8 ms.
stars_or_usage: 181 stars on the GitHub mirror; upstream is on SourceForge
tradeoffs: FFT-based oversampling plus bandlimited interpolation with configurable phase, bandwidth and rejection; multi-channel resampling can use several cores; higher latency than non-FFT resamplers (README: about 20 ms for the High Quality setting between 44.1 and 48 kHz); offers a libsamplerate-compatible header (soxr-lsr.h).
caveats: The numbers are third-party and measured through Python wrapper packages on a single short clip; python-soxr bundles a patched libsoxr and the Colab notebook linked from the README was not opened. Quality settings were not matched by SNR across libraries, and CPU model and flags are not stated. The libsoxr README's own 'fast' claim carries no comparison. The GitHub repo is a mirror whose last commit is from 2018.
found_via: WebSearch: "faster than libsamplerate" OR "faster than libsoxr" OR "faster than swresample" resampler github (python-soxr benchmark snippet), then raw READMEs of chirlu/soxr and dofuuz/python-soxr
